# SPD-095 — Bash hook Law 7: a clone into scratch is refused, so a member cannot reproduce a shallow-checkout condition

## Brief
Found on BAD-078 (2026-09-16). BADS-078/Katahdin was briefed to reproduce a CI failure caused by `actions/checkout`'s shallow clone, and the natural reproduction is a depth-1 clone from a local path into a scratch directory outside every registered project. The Bash hook refused it under Law 7, which holds the clone verb for any caller with an `agent_id`, with no exception for a target outside the projects.

The refusal is correct as the rule is written, and Katahdin handled it well — she named the refusal rather than skipping the verification or claiming it, and substituted a probe that produces the byte-identical failure class (git cannot distinguish a well-formed absent revision from a shallow-omitted object). But the substitution was hers to invent under time pressure, and the brief that promised her the clone was Spud's and was wrong.

The question this ticket asks: is the clone verb a write verb in the sense Law 7 means?

Law 7 exists so a spudagent never commits, never rewrites history, and never moves a checkout under Spud's feet. A clone into a scratch path does none of those. It creates a new repository nobody else reads, from a source it only reads. It is closer to the archive verb — already permitted, and already how members stage trees into scratch — than to the checkout verb. SPD-064 established that a member writing outside every registered project is a case the path rule has to reason about rather than refuse by accident, so there is precedent for the shape of the answer.

Against relaxing it: a clone whose TARGET is inside a project checkout really is a write there, and a clone can be pointed at a path that later gets committed. The verb also takes template and config options with hook-adjacent behaviour, which is the class of thing SPD-046 found under other verbs. So any relaxation has to be a target check rather than a verb exemption, and has to survive the expansion and substitution cases SPD-049, SPD-089 and SPD-091 name.

Decide one of: leave the verb refused and write the substitution into the guidance so a brief never promises it again; permit it when the target resolves outside every registered project and the source is read-only; or permit it only into the session's scratch directory specifically.

Whichever wins, the spudagent brief template or the laws should say so, because the failure mode here was a brief written against a rule Spud had misremembered.
